foundations.quizTarget: You edit the output value but run the old executable without rebuilding. What should you expect?

essentialSupport.fact: A compiler checks source code and translates it into a program the machine can run. A compilation error means no valid executable was produced from that attempt; it is different from a failure while a program runs.
#include <iostream> makes standard stream declarations available. std::cout is the output stream in the std namespace; :: selects a name from that namespace.
int main() is the entry function for this program. Its braces contain the instructions. Reaching the end of main returns a success status of zero.
The output below appears when the built executable runs, not merely when the source file is saved. A changed source file must be rebuilt before the executable reflects that edit.

foundations.reasoning: Editing source and rebuilding an executable are separate actions.

foundations.quizTarget: With denominator changed to zero, what happens?

essentialSupport.fact: bool holds true or false. && requires both conditions; || requires at least one; ! reverses a Boolean result.
&& skips its right side when the left side is false. || skips its right side when the left side is true. This short-circuit order can protect a risky operation.
denominator != 0 asks whether the value is nonzero. Put it before the division in an && expression so zero never reaches that division.
std::boolalpha makes the stream show true or false instead of numeric Boolean output. It changes the display, not the underlying result.

foundations.reasoning: The left condition already makes && false, so the risky right side is not evaluated.

foundations.quizTarget: Replace int count{3} with int count{3.5}. What happens?

essentialSupport.fact: int holds whole numbers within a finite range. double holds approximate fractional numbers. Initialize variables before reading them; braces such as int count{3} supply an initial value.
int count{3.5} is rejected because the fractional value would lose information. This is a compile-time error, not a runtime rounding instruction.

static_cast<int>(3.5) explicitly converts this in-range value to 3 by truncating toward zero. Do not use an out-of-range floating-to-integer conversion; it has undefined behavior, not a guaranteed wrap or exception.
5 / 2 uses integer division. 5.0 / 2.0 uses double operands and gives 2.5. Signed integer overflow is also undefined behavior; do not rely on wrapping.

foundations.reasoning: List initialization disallows this narrowing conversion rather than silently dropping the fraction.

foundations.quizTarget: Change the char initializer from single-quoted A to double-quoted A. What happens?

essentialSupport.fact: A single-quoted literal such as 'A' is a char. Double quotes such as "Moon" form a string literal. They are not interchangeable types.
std::string, declared in <string>, stores a sequence of char values and manages its storage. std::string name{"Moon"} creates an owning string value.
name.size() reports its number of char units. This is not necessarily the number of visible Unicode symbols when text uses a multi-unit encoding.
A char variable accepts a character value such as 'B'. Assigning a whole double-quoted string literal to it is not a valid substitute.

foundations.reasoning: Single and double quotes produce different kinds of values; the char variable cannot receive that string literal.

foundations.quizTarget: Add limit = 4 before the output. What happens?

essentialSupport.fact: const int limit{3} declares an integer that cannot be reassigned through that name. const applies to the declared object or access path; it is not a promise that all nearby data is fixed.
auto score = 2 asks the compiler to deduce int from the initializer. The type stays int afterward; normal conversion rules still apply to later assignments.
score can be replaced because it is not const. Reading limit in a calculation is allowed; assigning a new value to limit is rejected.

foundations.reasoning: The declaration made limit const; a later write through that name is not allowed.

foundations.quizTarget: Input -2 is a valid integer. Why does this program still reject it?

essentialSupport.fact: std::cin >> count attempts to extract an integer from standard input into count. Testing the stream in if reports whether extraction succeeded. For the worked example, type 3 and press Enter. A live terminal waits for input; end-of-input takes the failure branch.
A successfully extracted integer can still be unsuitable. count >= 0 rejects negative counts even though they are valid integers.
The && form checks extraction before the nonnegative rule. On extraction failure, use the error branch rather than assuming the stored number is valid.

Formatted extraction reads a numeric token, not a guarantee that the entire line contained only that number. Extra trailing characters can remain unread. This example ends after one attempt; a retry loop must also recover the stream state and discard unsuitable input.

foundations.reasoning: The input passes integer extraction but fails the application’s count rule.

foundations.quizTarget: Change choice to 9. Which output occurs?

essentialSupport.fact: switch selects a case based on an integral or enum value. case 1 labels the instructions for the value 1.
break exits this switch. Without it, execution can continue into following case instructions, even if their labels do not equal the original value.
default handles an input with no matching case label. It is separate from the numbered choices.
This beginner example uses break on each case to avoid accidental fallthrough. Do not remove a break unless continuing into the next block is the intended behavior.

foundations.reasoning: The default label handles this unmatched input.

foundations.quizTarget: Replace continue with break. What prints?

essentialSupport.fact: for (int i{0}; i < 4; ++i) initializes i once, tests before each body run, and increments after each body. ++i increases i by one.
continue skips the remaining body but still reaches the for-loop update before another test.
break leaves the loop immediately. It does not merely skip one printed value.
Initialization, test, body, update, and another test determine which values are visited. A skipped body remainder does not freeze the loop counter.

foundations.reasoning: 0 prints first, then break exits before the next value is printed.

foundations.quizTarget: After push_back, read at(2) instead of at(0). Which value is selected?

essentialSupport.fact: std::vector<int> stores a sequence of integers and manages its own storage. <vector> declares the type; the angle brackets select its element type.
push_back adds an element at the end. size() gives the number of currently stored elements, not an index.
at(0) reads the first element. at checks bounds and reports an out-of-range access by throwing; exception handling is taught later. operator[] does not provide that same check.
For three values, valid positions are 0, 1, and 2. Do not deliberately execute an invalid unchecked access.

foundations.reasoning: Zero-based positions identify the third appended value at index 2.

foundations.quizTarget: Change only the assigned position from at(1) to at(2). What happens to the printed second value and size?

essentialSupport.fact: std::array<int, 3> stores exactly three integers. Both the element type and the length are part of its type.
Writing values.at(1) replaces the second element. It does not add a fourth slot or change size().
The brace initializer supplies the starting values. Unlike vector, this container has no push_back operation to grow it.
at reports an invalid position instead of silently granting another slot. This example uses only positions known to be in bounds.

foundations.reasoning: The assignment targets the third slot; the second remains 4 and fixed size stays 3.

foundations.quizTarget: Use an empty vector while keeping total initialized to zero. What prints?

essentialSupport.fact: A range-for such as for (int score : scores) visits each value in the sequence and copies it into score for that pass.
A total initialized to zero can add each visited score. The source sequence is separate from the total variable.
Changing this by-value score does not change its corresponding element in scores. References, taught next, are needed for a loop variable that aliases an element.
For an empty vector the body runs zero times, so the initial accumulator stays unchanged.

foundations.reasoning: An empty sequence performs no body executions.

foundations.quizTarget: Replace int& alias with int alias. What happens after alias = 9?

essentialSupport.fact: int& alias = score binds alias to the existing score object. It is another name for that object, not an independent copied integer.
alias = 9 changes score because both names access the same object. A reference must be initialized when declared.
After binding, assigning another value through alias does not make it refer to a different variable. It changes the object it already names.
int copy = score creates a separate value. Changing copy later does not change score.

foundations.reasoning: Removing & changes this declaration from an alias to an independent int.

foundations.quizTarget: Add name.clear() inside show_size before the output. What happens?

essentialSupport.fact: A parameter const std::string& name refers to the caller’s string without copying it for the parameter. const prevents this function from modifying that string through this parameter.
The function may inspect the input during the call. It must not keep a borrowed reference for use after the original object has gone away.
size() can inspect a const string. Calling a mutating operation such as clear() through this const reference is rejected.
The complete example places the function definition before main, so its signature is known at the call site. void means this function returns no value; it displays the size instead.

foundations.reasoning: This is a reference rather than a copy, and its const access forbids mutation.

foundations.quizTarget: Replace the pointer initializer with nullptr. Which branch runs?

essentialSupport.fact: int* observer points to an int object. &score obtains score’s address. The pointer is a separate variable, not the integer object itself.
*observer accesses the pointed-to object. A pointer must refer to a suitable live object before you dereference it; being non-null alone is not proof of lifetime validity.
nullptr means the pointer has no object target. Test it before dereferencing when absence is possible.
This raw pointer only observes a local int. It does not allocate or own it, and must not delete it. Ownership is taught later with RAII and smart pointers.

foundations.reasoning: The explicit absence check chooses the else branch and avoids an invalid dereference.

foundations.quizTarget: Change the final output to inner instead of saved. What happens?

essentialSupport.fact: A local variable declared inside braces is visible only within its scope. Code outside that block cannot refer to its name.
For these ordinary local variables, the object’s lifetime ends when its block exits. A saved pointer or reference does not extend that lifetime.
Copying a small integer into an outer variable before the inner block ends gives the outer variable its own surviving value.
Returning a pointer or reference to an ordinary local object leaves a dangling observer after the function exits. Such code may compile but using it is unsafe; it is not a valid runtime experiment.

foundations.reasoning: The copied value remains in saved, but inner’s name is no longer in scope.

foundations.quizTarget: Change describe(4) to describe(std::string{"4"}). Which description is returned?

essentialSupport.fact: Functions may share a name when their parameter lists differ. An int argument can select an int overload while a string argument selects a string overload. These two example overloads do not use their input values, so their parameter names are omitted while their types remain declared.
Two functions cannot be distinguished merely by different return types with identical parameters. The call must have an unambiguous applicable signature.
A parameter such as int bonus = 1 uses that default when the argument is omitted. Passing zero explicitly is different from omitting the argument.
Avoid overlapping defaults that make a call ambiguous. In this example the bonus function has its own name, separate from the describe overloads.

foundations.reasoning: Overload selection uses argument types, not the appearance of the stored characters.

essentialSupport.fact: Recursion occurs when a function calls itself. Each call has its own parameter value and waits for a result from the smaller call.
If n <= 0 this function returns zero without another call. A reachable base case prevents unbounded recursive calls.
For a positive n, sum_down(n - 1) reduces the input. The current call adds its own n after that result returns.
Recursion uses finite call-stack space and integer results have finite ranges. This exercise uses only small inputs; it is not permission to test huge depths or overflow.

foundations.reasoning: The smaller input creates a shorter chain ending at the same base case.

foundations.quizTarget: Change the assignment to session.score = 5 instead. What does the output show?

essentialSupport.fact: enum class State { Ready, Done } creates named choices scoped under State. State::Ready is a typed value, not the text "Ready".
A struct can hold named members. Here Session contains a State and an int score. Its members are public by default.
Session session{State::Ready, 2} supplies the member values in their declaration order. The dot operator accesses a member such as session.score.
Assigning session.state = State::Done changes only that member. It does not automatically increase score or print a message.

foundations.reasoning: Each member is separate state; updating score does not alter the enum member.

ownership-and-generic.quizTarget: If both add(2) calls become add(1), what prints?

essentialSupport.fact: An invariant is a rule every usable object must maintain. This Counter permits values from 0 through 3. Private data prevents outside code from bypassing its checked operations.

class members are private until public: changes access. add returns false without changing value when a request would exceed 3. value += amount adds amount to the current value and stores the result. A trailing const on get() promises not to change this object through that member function.
std::boolalpha prints Boolean results as true or false. The two calls request 2, then 2 more; the second is rejected, so get() returns 2.

ownership-and-generic.reasoning: Both requests fit the invariant: 0→1→2. A rejection would leave the old value unchanged.

ownership-and-generic.quizTarget: Change Session s{12} to Session s{7}. What does duration return?

essentialSupport.fact: A constructor has the class name and no return type. It runs when an object is created. The : minutes{n} member initializer initializes minutes before the constructor body.

explicit prevents this one-argument constructor being used as an implicit conversion. Session s{12} deliberately constructs a Session. int minutes has no separate default initialization here: the initializer supplies it.
Members initialize in their declaration order, not the order you type in the initializer list. Use initializers for members, especially const or reference members that cannot be assigned later.

ownership-and-generic.reasoning: The constructor parameter n receives 7 and directly initializes minutes with that value.

ownership-and-generic.quizTarget: Insert return 0 inside the nested scope after work. What prints?

essentialSupport.fact: RAII means Resource Acquisition Is Initialization: an owning object acquires a resource during construction and releases it during destruction. A destructor is named ~ClassName and takes no arguments.

This Trace is a lifecycle illustration, not an actual file owner. Its constructor/destructor print when a nested scope begins and ends. Real standard-library owners use this lifetime mechanism to release memory or close handles.

Use standard containers and smart pointers instead of hand-writing ownership code. Automatic objects are destroyed in reverse construction order on normal scope exit. Cleanup destructors should not allow failures to escape.

ownership-and-generic.reasoning: Returning still exits the scope and destroys marker. The after statement is not reached. This is normal return, not abrupt process termination.

ownership-and-generic.quizTarget: Replace auto b = a with auto& b = a. What prints?

essentialSupport.fact: Copying a std::vector creates an independent vector with copies of its elements. auto b = a declares a new value; it is not a reference alias.
auto& b = a would make b another name for a. The ampersand changes ownership and mutation consequences. Here both indices are valid because each vector contains two elements.

ownership-and-generic.reasoning: b now aliases a, so assigning b[0] changes the same element observed through a[0].

ownership-and-generic.quizTarget: If b is copied from a instead, why does the final output still read 2 7?

essentialSupport.fact: std::move from <utility> does not itself move bytes or empty an object. It casts an expression so a receiving operation may use move semantics. Standard containers can transfer owned storage efficiently.

After moving this vector into b, b has the original values. The source vector remains valid but its value is unspecified; do not predict its size. Calling clear then push_back gives a a known new value.
Moving is not reference aliasing. Reusing a after resetting it does not change b. Small scalar moves can just copy; std::move is not a universal speed switch.

ownership-and-generic.reasoning: The final operations deliberately overwrite a’s contents, so the output does not reveal the different transfer/copy work.

ownership-and-generic.quizTarget: Make b a Notebook& alias. How do the reported sizes change?

essentialSupport.fact: The rule of zero: when standard owning members already manage resources, avoid defining custom destructors, copy operations or move operations just to repeat that work.

Notebook contains a std::string and std::vector. Their generated memberwise copy gives an independent name and vector. A struct makes members public by default; braces supply members in declaration order.

Rule of zero is a design preference, not a ban on destructors. A class directly managing a special handle needs deliberate ownership design. Merely adding a destructor can also affect automatic move generation.

ownership-and-generic.reasoning: An alias does not copy the member vector. push_back then changes the single original Notebook.

ownership-and-generic.quizTarget: Replace std::move(p) with p when initializing q. What happens?

essentialSupport.fact: std::unique_ptr<T> from <memory> owns one object and destroys it automatically. std::make_unique<int>(7) constructs a heap-allocated int and returns its owner. Prefer this to raw owning new/delete.
unique_ptr cannot be copied. Moving it transfers ownership and specifically leaves the source pointer empty. Test a pointer before dereferencing it; *q accesses its owned int.
In a condition a nonempty smart pointer is true. The comparison p == nullptr checks whether p is empty; this check does not access a missing object.

ownership-and-generic.reasoning: Copy construction is deleted. Shared ownership requires a different, deliberate type, not a copied unique_ptr.

ownership-and-generic.quizTarget: Omit second.reset(). What does expired() report?

essentialSupport.fact: Copies of std::shared_ptr participate in shared ownership. The object remains alive while at least one owning shared_ptr remains. std::make_shared constructs the object and shared ownership state.

std::weak_ptr does not own the object. lock() returns a temporary shared_ptr if the object is still alive, or an empty one otherwise. reset() releases one owner, not all owners. In if (auto live = observer.lock()), the condition declares live, tests whether it is nonempty, and limits its lifetime to that if statement. expired() reports whether no owning shared_ptr remains.
If objects own one another through shared_ptr, the cycle can prevent destruction. A weak back-reference can break the cycle. Prefer unique ownership when sharing is unnecessary.

ownership-and-generic.reasoning: The weak observer does not own the int, but second does. The temporary live owner is scoped to the if statement.

ownership-and-generic.quizTarget: If Square::score returns 6, what does show print through Shape&?

essentialSupport.fact: A virtual member can select an override based on the actual object type. = 0 makes score() pure virtual: Shape is abstract and cannot be instantiated directly.

struct Square : Shape publicly derives from Shape. override asks the compiler to verify that the signature really overrides a virtual function. Passing const Shape& preserves the actual Square object. Shape itself is abstract, so creating a Shape value is ill-formed. With a concrete base type, copying a derived object into a base value can instead slice away the derived part.

virtual ~Shape() = default declares a virtual destructor with compiler-provided behavior. Its importance when deleting through a base owner is the next lesson. score() const can be called through a const base reference.

ownership-and-generic.reasoning: An abstract base reference can refer to a concrete derived object. The virtual call selects that object’s override.

ownership-and-generic.quizTarget: Call owner.reset() twice. How many times does derived print?

essentialSupport.fact: A unique_ptr<Base> may own a Derived object. For ordinary deletion through Base*, Base needs a virtual destructor so derived cleanup happens too. Removing it here would be undefined behavior; we do not run that variant.
reset() destroys the currently owned object and empties the pointer. Derived destruction runs before Base destruction. Logging is only a visible demonstration of cleanup order.
Resetting an already-empty unique_ptr does nothing. This can be tested without invoking undefined behavior.

ownership-and-generic.reasoning: The first reset destroys the derived object through the virtual destructor. The empty second reset owns nothing to destroy.

ownership-and-generic.quizTarget: Replace larger(2, 5) with larger(2, 5.0). What happens?

essentialSupport.fact: template<typename T> introduces a type parameter named T. The compiler instantiates a concrete function for a chosen type. This is compile-time generic code, not a runtime dynamically typed function.

larger(2, 5) deduces T as int. Both parameters use the same T. Passing one int and one double does not silently choose a common type for this signature; deduction conflicts unless the caller supplies a suitable explicit type.

This version returns by value, not a borrowed reference. These numeric examples copy values; other types may use move operations when returning a parameter. The comparison and value construction operations must be valid for the chosen type. Later a concept will state a constraint explicitly.

ownership-and-generic.reasoning: The same T would need to be int and double. An explicit larger<double>(2,5.0) could request conversion, but is not the changed call.

ownership-and-generic.quizTarget: Change ratio to Box<int> but keep {1.5}. What happens?

essentialSupport.fact: template<typename T> can parameterize a class. Box<int> and Box<double> are distinct types. Each stores a T and exposes a copy through get().

Box(T value) : item{value} initializes the member using the constructor input. explicit keeps construction deliberate. We spell the template argument at the call site rather than introducing class-template deduction here.

ownership-and-generic.reasoning: The explicit type selects an int constructor parameter; brace initialization rejects this double-to-int narrowing.

ownership-and-generic.quizTarget: Change twice(3) to twice(2.5). What occurs?

essentialSupport.fact: A concept is a compile-time constraint. <concepts> supplies std::integral, which accepts integral types such as int but not double. template<std::integral T> constrains the type parameter.
Constraints improve which calls are permitted; they do not prove all runtime inputs safe. This doubling example uses small values whose result fits int. Unchecked signed overflow is not allowed.
Calling twice with 2.5 fails constraint checking instead of quietly truncating it. There is no successful runtime result for that changed program.

ownership-and-generic.reasoning: Deduction selects double, which does not satisfy std::integral. Constraints are checked before execution.

ownership-and-generic.quizTarget: Change the capture to [&offset]. What prints in this same scope?

essentialSupport.fact: A lambda is an unnamed function object. [offset](int value) { return value + offset; } takes an int and captures a copy of offset at creation. auto holds the lambda’s generated type.
[&offset] captures a reference instead. It observes later changes but must not outlive offset. Do not return or store a reference-capturing lambda past the referenced object’s lifetime.
The parameter value arrives on each call; the capture supplies surrounding context. Changing offset after value capture does not change the stored copy.

ownership-and-generic.reasoning: The reference capture sees the current offset of 5 when add(3) runs; both objects are still alive.

ownership-and-generic.quizTarget: Replace the second lambda assignment with operation = nullptr. What prints?

essentialSupport.fact: std::function<int(int)> from <functional> stores a copyable callable taking an int and returning an int. It can hold different compatible lambda types behind one declared type. The empty [] capture list means this lambda uses no surrounding local variables.
auto is simpler when the concrete callable type need not change. std::function adds flexibility with possible overhead. Calling an empty std::function throws; check it in a condition before calling.
Assigning a new compatible lambda replaces the old target. Captures still obey their own lifetime rules; the wrapper does not make borrowed references safe.

ownership-and-generic.reasoning: The first call already printed 4. Clearing the wrapper makes the following Boolean check false, so there is no empty call.

ownership-and-generic.quizTarget: Replace the two values with an empty vector. What prints?

essentialSupport.fact: begin() identifies the first element; end() identifies one past the last. The notation [begin, end) includes begin but excludes end. Never dereference end.
An iterator supports operations appropriate to its category. Here ++it moves to the next vector element and *it accesses the current element. Compare to end before dereferencing.
For an empty vector, begin() equals end(), so this loop executes zero times. No special dereference is needed to discover emptiness.

ownership-and-generic.reasoning: begin equals end before the first iteration, and total was initialized to zero.

ownership-and-generic.quizTarget: Search for 9 instead of 4. Which branch runs?

essentialSupport.fact: std::find from <algorithm> searches [first,last) for the first equal value. It returns an iterator to that element, or last if there is no match.
The result is not a Boolean and is not automatically safe to dereference. Comparing it to values.end() distinguishes a match from absence. The vector remains unchanged.

ownership-and-generic.reasoning: No element equals 9, so find returns the end iterator and the guard prevents dereferencing it.

ownership-and-generic.quizTarget: Replace a > b with a < b. What sequence prints?

essentialSupport.fact: std::sort rearranges a random-access range such as vector iterators. A comparison callable answers whether the first value should come before the second.

a > b requests descending numeric order; a < b requests ascending order. A valid comparator must provide a strict weak ordering: never put a before itself, and keep ordering/equivalence consistent. Do not use <= or >= as a sort comparator.
An invalid comparator violates the algorithm’s requirements; its result is not a harmless alternative ordering. We test < versus >, not an invalid comparator.

ownership-and-generic.reasoning: The comparator now places smaller numbers before larger ones; sort mutates the vector into ascending order.

ownership-and-generic.quizTarget: Start accumulation at 10 rather than 0. What prints?

essentialSupport.fact: std::transform applies a callable to each input and writes one result per element. The output vector is constructed with values.size() elements; merely reserving capacity would not create writable elements.
std::accumulate from <numeric> combines elements, starting with an initial accumulator. The initial value also determines its type. Here 0 is int and the small sum fits int.
The transform writes into doubled, leaving values unchanged. Accumulation computes one result rather than modifying the vector.

ownership-and-generic.reasoning: The doubled values are 2,4,6. The initial accumulator participates in the sum: 10+2+4+6=22.

ownership-and-generic.quizTarget: Change the filter from x > 1 to x > 2. What is traversed?

essentialSupport.fact: A range view describes iteration rather than eagerly creating a new vector. std::views::filter keeps values satisfying a predicate; std::views::transform computes a value from each kept element. | composes these adaptors.
The for loop traverses the pipeline: filter values greater than 1, then multiply each by 10. The underlying vector remains 1,2,3. This example does not modify it while a view is being traversed.
This view refers to the named vector, which outlives traversal. Do not return this view from a function if its local vector would be destroyed. Avoid assuming views are cached result collections.

ownership-and-generic.reasoning: Only source value 3 passes the new predicate; the transform then yields 30.

ownership-and-generic.quizTarget: Use a vector containing only 2, then erase it. What prints?

essentialSupport.fact: A vector operation can invalidate iterators, references and pointers into its elements. Reallocation during growth invalidates all of them. erase invalidates positions at and after the erased element.
vector::erase returns a fresh iterator to the element following the erased one, or end if there is none. Replace the old iterator with that result and check end before dereferencing.
Using an invalidated iterator is not a reliable way to see an old value; it can be undefined behavior. This example only reads the newly returned valid position.

ownership-and-generic.reasoning: After erasing the sole element the vector is empty. The returned iterator equals end, so the guard selects the end branch.

library-and-concurrency.quizTarget: Replace the find/first-print statements with std::cout << scores["Zed"] << " " << scores.size() << "\n";. What changes?

essentialSupport.fact: A std::map<Key,Value> keeps one value for each distinct key and visits keys in comparator order. Here strings use their usual lexicographic ordering, so Ada comes before Mina, regardless of insertion order.
find(key) returns an iterator or end() when absent. Comparing with end() before dereferencing avoids using a missing element. find does not add a key.
operator[] is different: scores["Zed"] inserts the missing key with a value-initialized int, which is 0. Use find or contains for observation; use [] when insertion is intended.
The structured binding const auto& [name, score] gives names to the existing pair’s key and value. It does not copy the whole map. The map key cannot be reassigned through this pair.

library-and-concurrency.reasoning: Indexing inserts Zed with int value 0. The later size is 3, and ordered iteration now includes that key.

library-and-concurrency.quizTarget: Replace the contains line with ++visits["lake"]; bool present = visits.contains("lake");. What prints?

essentialSupport.fact: An unordered_map associates keys with values using a hash function and key equality. Lookup is average constant time, but worst-case linear; that is not a promise about wall-clock speed.
Its iteration order is not sorted or insertion order. Rehashing may change that order and invalidate iterators. Do not use an observed order as the expected answer of a portable program.
contains(key) reports whether the key exists without changing the map. As with map, [] inserts a missing key and value-initializes the value; ++visits["lake"] therefore changes a new 0 to 1.

library-and-concurrency.reasoning: The indexed increment creates lake with 0, increments it to 1, and leaves two keys. contains then returns true.

library-and-concurrency.quizTarget: Change badges.insert(3) to badges.insert(2). What prints before the iteration line?

essentialSupport.fact: A std::set<T> stores distinct keys in comparator order. With the default integer comparison, {3,1,3} contains only 1 and 3. It does not remember a count of repeated 3 values.
insert(value) returns a pair: first identifies the existing or added element, and second is true only when a new element was inserted. Duplicate insertion leaves the size unchanged.
The set’s values are its keys. Changing a stored value directly would break ordering; erase the old value and insert a new value instead.

library-and-concurrency.reasoning: 2 was absent, so insertion succeeds and raises the number of distinct keys from two to three.

library-and-concurrency.quizTarget: Change reward(true) to reward(false). Which branch runs, and why?

essentialSupport.fact: std::optional<int> holds either an int or no value. std::nullopt constructs the empty state; it does not mean the integer zero.

In if(result), optional converts to true when a value is present, even when that value is 0. Only dereference *result after establishing presence; dereferencing an empty optional is not a safe fallback.
value_or(defaultValue) can supply a fallback without altering the optional. It is useful only when treating absence as that fallback fits the application.

library-and-concurrency.reasoning: false selects nullopt. The condition checks presence, not the numeric truthiness of an int.

library-and-concurrency.quizTarget: Initialize message with std::string{"ready"} instead of 7. What prints?

essentialSupport.fact: std::variant<int,std::string> normally owns one of those two alternatives at a time. Assigning a string replaces the int alternative; it does not retain both payloads.
std::get_if<int>(&message) returns a pointer to the int when it is active, otherwise nullptr. The if checks that pointer before dereferencing it.

std::get<T> throws std::bad_variant_access for the wrong active alternative. This example’s else knows the other alternative because these simple assignments succeed. A variant can become valueless after certain throwing operations; general code must account for that possibility.

library-and-concurrency.reasoning: The string is now active, so get_if<int> returns null and the string branch prints its value.

library-and-concurrency.quizTarget: Change twice(4) to twice(-1). What does the caller do?

essentialSupport.fact: C++23 std::expected<T,E> contains either a successful T or an error E. It is useful when the caller should inspect a recoverable failure as part of the function’s return contract.
std::unexpected("outside range") selects the error alternative here. The function accepts only 0 through 100, so multiplication in its successful branch is safe for int.

if(result) checks for success; *result accesses that successful int. error() is used only in the error branch. expected does not make other operations magically nonthrowing, and blindly accessing the wrong alternative is not a recovery strategy.

library-and-concurrency.reasoning: The range guard returns unexpected before multiplication; the caller explicitly selects and prints the error alternative.

library-and-concurrency.quizTarget: Pass -1 instead of 3 to checkedReward. Which output is correct?

essentialSupport.fact: throw signals a failure and transfers control toward a matching handler. Statements after the throwing operation inside that try block are skipped; a failed call does not supply its normal return value.

try encloses work that this boundary can handle. catch(const std::invalid_argument& error) handles that exception type without copying it. what() provides a descriptive string, not a machine-readable application protocol.

When stack unwinding occurs, destructors of fully constructed automatic objects in exited scopes run. Prefer RAII for cleanup. After this handler finishes normally, execution continues after the catch; an uncaught exception can terminate the program.

library-and-concurrency.reasoning: The throw skips the reward print. The matching handler prints the rejection, then execution continues after the boundary.

library-and-concurrency.quizTarget: Instead, push directly into scores, then throw for a negative value, with no rollback. After adding -2, what does the catch leave?

essentialSupport.fact: The basic exception guarantee preserves valid invariants and avoids resource leaks, but may leave changed values. The strong guarantee additionally leaves the protected operation’s state unchanged when it fails.

addValidated builds a separate vector candidate. Copying, allocation or validation can fail before scores is changed. The final swap commits the prepared result; swapping these default-allocator vectors does not throw.

Replacing the candidate operations with direct edits to scores changes the guarantee. Catching the validation exception does not undo a previously successful push_back. noexcept also does not mean success: an escaping exception from a noexcept function terminates.

library-and-concurrency.reasoning: The direct push already succeeded. The catch handles control flow but supplies no rollback, so the strong guarantee has been lost.

library-and-concurrency.quizTarget: Replace run.txt with run.dat. Does this create a file, and which extension prints?

essentialSupport.fact: std::filesystem::path represents a filesystem path. Constructing it does not create, open or verify a file. generic_string uses a generic slash-separated spelling for display.

lexically_normal simplifies dot and dot-dot components without consulting the filesystem. It does not resolve symlinks or prove the destination exists; real canonicalization and access checks are separate operations.
extension() inspects the final filename’s extension. Filesystem operations that touch disk can fail or race with other processes; choosing a path object is not permission to overwrite a real file.

library-and-concurrency.reasoning: Only lexical path manipulation occurs. The final filename ends in .dat, but no I/O operation has been requested.

library-and-concurrency.quizTarget: Open only the second output stream with std::ios::app. What text is read after both writes succeed?

essentialSupport.fact: This example creates or overwrites practice.txt in the current working directory. Run it only in a disposable folder; the test harness supplies one. Existing personal files are never needed.
An ofstream opened this way truncates an existing file. std::ios::app instead writes at the end. Neither insertion of a string nor opening in append mode adds a newline automatically.

if(!out) checks stream failure. Explicit close followed by a state check can detect a failed final write; destruction still closes resources through RAII, but does not report successful persistence to the caller. ifstream and getline also need success checks.

library-and-concurrency.reasoning: Appending preserves first and adds the exact characters second. Neither write supplied a newline.

library-and-concurrency.quizTarget: Replace owner[0] = 'F'; with owner[1] = 'O';. After remove_prefix(1), what does the last line show?

essentialSupport.fact: std::string_view stores a pointer and length, not an owning string copy. Its owner must remain alive and its storage must remain valid while the view is used.

Assigning owner[0] changes an existing character without reallocating storage. The view sees that edit. Operations that replace or grow the owner may invalidate the view; do not keep a view into a destroyed temporary string.

remove_prefix shortens the view, not the owning string. It requires that the removed count is no greater than the view length. A string_view also need not end with a null character; data() is not automatically a C-string.

library-and-concurrency.reasoning: The borrowed characters reflect the owner’s O. Removing the view’s prefix hides only the first character from the view; the owner stays fOrest.

library-and-concurrency.quizTarget: Change only the function parameter to std::span<const int>. What happens to values[0] = 9?

essentialSupport.fact: std::span<T> views consecutive elements with a length. Here it borrows a std::array without copying or owning the elements. The storage must remain alive and uninvalidated while the span is used.

A span<int> permits writes to the original ints. Passing the lightweight span by value copies the view, not the array. The empty check ensures index zero exists; C++23 operator[] does not provide a mandatory bounds-checked exception.
std::span<const int> forbids changing elements through that view. const std::span<int> would instead make the view object const while leaving its int elements mutable. Neither form takes ownership.

library-and-concurrency.reasoning: The viewed element type is const int, so assignment is ill-formed; no runtime attempt is needed.

library-and-concurrency.quizTarget: Change twice(3) to twice(4) but keep static_assert(size == 6). What happens?

essentialSupport.fact: A constexpr function can participate in constant evaluation when its inputs and operations permit it. Calling that function does not by itself force every call to happen at compile time.
constexpr int size = twice(3) requires a constant expression. By contrast, an ordinary int can hold a runtime result even when the called function is declared constexpr.
static_assert requires a constant condition. A false condition rejects the program during compilation, before main runs. This is different from a runtime assert that may be disabled in some builds.

library-and-concurrency.reasoning: size becomes the constant 8. The required compile-time assertion 8 == 6 is false.

library-and-concurrency.quizTarget: Remove the guard lines from score.hpp but keep both includes. What happens in this translation unit?

essentialSupport.fact: A header is text included into a translation unit (one source file after preprocessing its includes). A declaration tells the compiler about a name and its type. A class definition such as struct Score may also live in a header when the language’s definition rules are respected.

Save this as score.hpp beside main.cpp:
```cpp
#ifndef SCORE_HPP
#define SCORE_HPP
struct Score { int value; };
#endif
```
The first inclusion defines SCORE_HPP. On the second inclusion, #ifndef is false, so the guarded definition is skipped. These preprocessor directives are not runtime if statements.

The source below intentionally includes the header twice. Compile main.cpp with the header available to the compiler. Use standard include guards rather than relying on a particular compiler’s #pragma once extension for this example.

library-and-concurrency.reasoning: Both include directives now paste the same struct definition into one translation unit. That is a redefinition, not a second execution.

library-and-concurrency.quizTarget: Build only main.cpp, with bonus.hpp present but without compiling/linking bonus.cpp. What fails?

essentialSupport.fact: A translation unit is a source file after preprocessing its includes. Compiling main.cpp can succeed because the compiler sees addBonus’s declaration; that alone does not supply its executable definition.

Build this example with g++ -std=c++23 main.cpp bonus.cpp -o example. Omitting bonus.cpp leaves the call without a supplied definition at link time. Giving the same ordinary function multiple definitions in separate files also violates the intended one-definition arrangement.

library-and-concurrency.reasoning: The declaration lets the call compile. The missing definition leaves an unresolved reference during linking.

library-and-concurrency.quizTarget: With this course’s -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Werror flags, add int unused = 7; inside main and never use it. What should you do with the build result?

essentialSupport.fact: Use -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic to request useful GCC diagnostics. They do not mean every possible warning is enabled. This course also uses -Werror, which treats emitted warnings as build errors rather than silently accepting them.

A local build with -g -fsanitize=address,undefined can instrument checks for supported memory and undefined-behavior errors. It only checks paths that actually execute; a clean run does not prove the whole program safe. Tool availability and platform support matter.

The worked array iteration stays in bounds. We do not execute invalid indexing or dangling-pointer examples. To demonstrate a rejected build safely, the changed case adds a genuinely unused variable; the configured warning policy rejects it before any run.

library-and-concurrency.reasoning: GCC diagnoses the unused local, and -Werror makes that diagnostic a compilation failure. Fix the cause or justify a deliberate policy change; do not pretend a binary was produced.

library-and-concurrency.quizTarget: Change the middle assertion to doubleSmall(2) == 5 and define NDEBUG before <cassert>. What can the final message prove?

essentialSupport.fact: An assertion states a condition that must hold at that point. These small tests cover zero, positive and negative inputs within a safe integer range; they are not exhaustive proof for every int.

With assertions enabled, a false assert prints a diagnostic and aborts. Keep tests small enough that a failure points toward a specific expectation. Production test frameworks can report many cases more conveniently.

Defining NDEBUG before including <cassert> disables assert checks. The expression is not evaluated then, so never put required side effects inside assert. A success message printed by a build with disabled assertions is not evidence that those conditions were checked.

library-and-concurrency.reasoning: NDEBUG disables the assert expressions. The displayed message cannot certify checks that were compiled out.

library-and-concurrency.quizTarget: Change 1750 milliseconds to 2500 milliseconds. What whole-seconds count prints?

essentialSupport.fact: std::chrono::duration represents a count together with a tick period. milliseconds{1750} is not the bare integer 1750 seconds. count() returns the stored count in that duration’s own unit.
duration_cast<seconds> converts this integer millisecond duration to whole seconds. The fractional part is discarded toward zero, so 1750 milliseconds becomes 1 second, not a rounded 2.

For real elapsed timing, subtract two steady_clock::now() time points and convert the resulting duration. A monotonic clock is suited to elapsed time, but workload timings still vary; this deterministic example converts a supplied duration instead of promising a benchmark result.

library-and-concurrency.reasoning: Integer duration_cast discards the fractional 0.5 second; it does not round to the nearest integer.

library-and-concurrency.quizTarget: Change die to {4,4} and replace the range check with roll == 4. What does the check print?

essentialSupport.fact: A random engine supplies pseudorandom state transitions. A distribution maps those engine results to values for a requested distribution. uniform_int_distribution<int>{1,6} includes both endpoints.

Seeding mt19937 with 42 gives the engine a repeatable initial state. Distribution algorithms can differ across standard-library implementations, so do not require the same displayed dice sequence on every toolchain.

This example checks that every generated value stays in the inclusive interval. Twenty rolls cannot establish that a generator is statistically fair, and mt19937 is not a cryptographic generator. Use application-appropriate randomness rather than a security claim.

library-and-concurrency.reasoning: The distribution’s only possible value is 4. No particular random engine sequence is needed to justify the result.

library-and-concurrency.quizTarget: Change the worker assignment to result = 12, keeping the scopes. May the final output still be the initial 0 because scheduling is slow?

essentialSupport.fact: A std::jthread starts work whose scheduling is independent of the following statements. Do not assume the worker has already completed just because its constructor returned.

When a joinable jthread is destroyed, it requests stop and joins. Joining waits for that thread to finish. A stop request is cooperative, not forced interruption; this small lambda simply returns normally.

The zero-argument lambda [&result] { ... } captures result by reference; the empty parameter list () is optional here. result is outside the worker’s scope, so it remains alive until after the worker is joined. The main thread reads it only after joining; it does not race with the worker’s write.

library-and-concurrency.reasoning: The join finishes the worker before the read. The reference points to the same still-live result, so the assigned 12 is observed.

library-and-concurrency.quizTarget: Remove only the finalLock line, keeping every worker lock and both joins. Is the final read safe?

essentialSupport.fact: Concurrent conflicting access to a non-atomic object, without the required synchronization, can be a data race and undefined behavior. We do not run an unlocked competing-write example.

The lambda capture [&] borrows the surrounding locals it uses by reference; count and mutex remain alive beyond both joins. Every worker increment here holds the same mutex. lock_guard locks on construction and unlocks on destruction, including when its scope exits. Its lifetime covers the entire ++count operation, not only a separate read.

Both jthreads are destroyed and joined before the final read. Therefore no worker still writes count at that point. The final read’s extra lock is harmless but unnecessary here; removing the worker locks would be a different, unsafe change.

library-and-concurrency.reasoning: Joining both workers ends the concurrent writes before the final read. The worker increments remain synchronized.

library-and-concurrency.quizTarget: Change only the final fetch_add(3) to fetch_add(5). Which pair prints?

essentialSupport.fact: std::atomic<int> supports indivisible accesses to this one counter. fetch_add(1) is an atomic read-modify-write: competing updates do not lose an increment as a separate load followed by store could.
fetch_add(amount) adds amount but returns the previous value. After both workers finish 100 increments, fetch_add(3) returns 200 while the counter becomes 203.

This example keeps the default sequentially consistent ordering. It does not teach custom memory-order or lock-free design. Individual atomic variables do not automatically preserve a multi-variable invariant; mutex-protected groups of operations may still be needed.

library-and-concurrency.reasoning: fetch_add still returns the old 200 and atomically raises the counter by 5 to 205.

library-and-concurrency.quizTarget: Change the last async argument from false to true. Where is calculation failed handled?

essentialSupport.fact: std::async returns a future associated with the invoked function’s result. Explicit std::launch::async requests asynchronous execution rather than leaving the choice between deferred and asynchronous policy to the implementation.
future::get waits as necessary and retrieves the value. For an ordinary future it consumes the result; do not call get a second time as if it were a reusable cache.

If the asynchronous function throws, the exception is stored and rethrown when get retrieves the result. Catch it around get when this boundary can handle it. Asynchronous execution does not guarantee better performance or a particular completion time.

library-and-concurrency.reasoning: The worker stores its exception in the shared result state. get rethrows it into the caller’s matching catch.

library-and-concurrency.quizTarget: Change the second command from collect to quit, leaving the final collect. What state prints?

essentialSupport.fact: This tiny console model receives a command and returns the next Game value. apply takes state by value, so the caller must assign the returned state. Fixed test commands replace interactive input; this is not a graphics engine.

The initial state has two turns. A collect command increases score and consumes one turn; reaching zero stops play. quit stops without consuming a turn, and an unknown command leaves state unchanged. Once stopped, later commands do nothing.

For states reached from this initializer, at most two successful collects occur, so the score and turn arithmetic stays bounded. Test early quit, unknown commands and extra commands after stopping. A production app must also validate state loaded from untrusted storage; this function does not accept arbitrary states as valid.

library-and-concurrency.reasoning: The first collect leaves score 1 and one turn. quit sets playing false without changing turns; the final command cannot change a stopped state.
